 1   I.      INTRODUCTION
 2           1.       This class action arises out of Wells Fargo’s drastic under-payment of interest to
 3   its own customers in its cash sweep program. Wells Fargo underpaid its customers in violation
 4   of its fiduciary and contractual duties in order to enrich itself at its customers’ expense. Rather
 5   than pay its customers a reasonable rate of interest on their cash as it was required to do, Wells
 6   Fargo instead paid miniscule rates to its customers, while it earned hundreds of millions of
 7   dollars on that cash due to rising interest rates.
 8           2.       In a typical cash sweep program for a brokerage customer, the brokerage firm
 9   moves uninvested cash from a customer’s brokerage account into an interest-bearing account that
10   generates returns for the client. When Wells Fargo sweeps its customers’ cash into its cash
11   sweep program, Wells Fargo uses that cash to generate outsized returns for itself, due to the
12   spread between the interest income that Wells Fargo earns on the cash in high interest rate
13   environments, and the amount of interest that it pays its clients.
14           3.       Wells Fargo is required to act as a fiduciary in the best interests of its clients.
15   That includes a duty to put its customers’ interests ahead of its own when recommending and
16   making investments for them. Wells Fargo explicitly promised to pay its clients with Wells
17   Fargo retirement accounts a “reasonable rate” of interest when Wells Fargo sweeps their cash
18   into its cash sweep program. In addition, under the law, the agreement between Wells Fargo and
19   its clients carries with it an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. That includes an
20   implied promise that neither party will do anything to frustrate the fruits of customers’ bargain
21   with Wells Fargo.
22           4.       Rather than act as a fiduciary in the best interests of Wells Fargo’s account
23   holders, or fulfill its contractual and implied covenant obligations to its customers, Wells Fargo
24   used its customers’ funds to enrich itself at the expense of its own clients.
25           5.       Rising interest rates presented an opportunity for Wells Fargo customers to earn
26   more on their cash sweep account balances. By improperly keeping the interest rates paid on
27   cash sweep accounts low, Wells Fargo usurped that opportunity for itself, leveraging its own
28   clients’ cash for its own benefit and earning near-guaranteed outsize returns year after year.

                                                          1
                                         CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 1          6.       For example, the yield on short-term U.S. Treasury bills increased dramatically

 2   over the past two years, and it has been above 5.25% for most of the past year. By contrast,

 3   during much of 2023, Wells Fargo paid customers with cash sweep accounts (and assets at Wells

 4   Fargo of up to $999,999) an interest rate of only 0.15%. That is more than 36 times less than the

 5   short-term Treasury Bill rate at the time. At present, Wells Fargo pays such accountholders only

 6   .02% interest on their cash sweep account balances. That is more than 234 times less than the

 7   prevailing short-term Treasury Bill yield.

 8          7.       There is nothing “reasonable” or “fair” about those rates, or about Wells Fargo

 9   using its clients’ cash balances to reap windfall profits at these disproportionate spreads. In stark

10   contrast, Fidelity—a Wells Fargo competitor—automatically sweeps uninvested cash in its

11   clients’ brokerage accounts into a money market fund currently earning approximately 5%.

12   Wells Fargo’s misconduct was a breach of its fiduciary duties, a breach of its contracts with

13   retirement fund account holders, and a breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair

14   dealing.

15          8.       Wells Fargo’s misconduct related to its cash sweep accounts has come under

16   scrutiny from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”). In the fall of 2023, Wells

17   Fargo disclosed that the SEC had launched an investigation into the cash sweep options that

18   Wells Fargo provided to its advisory clients. Wells Fargo later disclosed on August 1, 2024, that

19   it “is in resolution discussions with the SEC.”

20          9.       Amid the SEC investigation, Wells Fargo announced on July 12, 2024, that it was

21   changing the rates “in wealth and investment management on sweep deposits and advisory

22   brokerage accounts.” Wells Fargo Chief Financial Officer Michael Santomassimo said that this

23   change “better aligns [with] rates paid in money market funds and is expected to reduce net

24   interest income by approximately $350 million this year.” This highlights the massive income

25   that Wells Fargo gains at the expense of customers.

26          10.      Plaintiff, individually and on behalf of the proposed Class and Subclasses defined

27   herein, brings this class action to remedy the significant financial harm caused by the

28   Defendants’ use of the Wells Fargo cash sweep program to enrich Wells Fargo at the cost of its

 1   own clients.

 2   II.    JURISDICTION AND VENUE

 3          11.     This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over Plaintiffs’ and the Class’s claims

 4   pursuant to the Class Action Fairness Act, including 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d). The matter in

 5   controversy exceeds the sum or value of $5,000,000, exclusive of interest and costs, and Plaintiff

 6   and other class members are a citizen of States different from the Defendants.

 7          12.     This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendants because Wells Fargo is

 8   headquartered in San Francisco and it conducts substantial business in this District.

 9          13.     Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b).

10   III.   PARTIES

11          A.      Plaintiff

12          14.     Plaintiff Darren Cobb is a citizen of Nevada, who maintained a Traditional
13   Individual Retirement Account (“IRA”) that was managed by Defendant Wells Fargo Clearing
14   Services, LLC d/b/a Wells Fargo Advisors (“Wells Fargo Advisors”). The cash balances in his
15   account were, at times, swept into Wells Fargo’s Bank Deposit Sweep Program (the “Cash
16   Sweep Program”).
17          B.      Defendants
18          15.     Defendant Wells Fargo & Company operates as a diversified financial services
19   company. It is incorporated in Delaware and has its principal place of business in San Francisco,
20   California, from where it provides banking, insurance, investments, mortgage, leasing, credit
21   cards, and consumer finance services. Wells Fargo & Company provides these services through
22   its subsidiaries (including Wells Fargo Advisors), and its Wealth and Investment Management
23   segment provides customers with investment management and fiduciary services.
24          16.     Defendant Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. provides Wells Fargo & Company’s personal
25   and commercial banking services. It is Wells Fargo & Company’s wholly-owned, national
26   banking subsidiary with its principal place of business in San Francisco, California. As of
27   December 31, 2023, Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. had assets of $1.7 trillion, or 90% of Wells Fargo
28   & Company’s assets. As the parent corporation of Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., Wells Fargo &

                                                      3
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
               Case 3:24-cv-06696-DMR Document 1 Filed 09/24/24 Page 5 of 24



 1   Company exercises control over the operations of Defendant Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., dictates

 2   the policies, procedures, and practices of Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., exercises power and control

 3   over the specific activities upon which the claims herein are based, and received the benefits of

 4   the wrongful conduct alleged herein.

 5          17.     Defendant Wells Fargo Advisors is a registered broker-dealer and provides

 6   brokerage and investment advisory services. It is a Delaware limited liability company and has

 7   its principal place of business in St. Louis, Missouri. It is a subsidiary of Wells Fargo &

 8   Company, which owns 75% or more of Wells Fargo Advisors. As the owner of Wells Fargo

 9   Advisors, Wells Fargo & Company directs the management and policies of Wells Fargo

10   Advisors.

11          18.     Wells Fargo and Company, Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., and Wells Fargo Advisors,

12   are referred to collectively herein as “Wells Fargo” or “Defendants.”

13   IV.    FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

14          A.      Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep Programs

15          19.     Net interest income is the difference between how much interest banks earn on
16   loans and investments, and how much they pay out to depositors. Wells Fargo is motivated to
17   increase its net interest income by depressing the value of the interest that it pays to its
18   customers, while taking advantage of the interest that Wells Fargo itself earns on the higher rates
19   that it receives on the customer cash that is held at Wells Fargo.
20          20.     Wells Fargo has two different cash sweep programs: (i) the Expanded Bank
21   Deposit Sweep; and (ii) the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep, for those customers who elect not to
22   participate in the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep. Collectively, these are referred to herein as
23   the “Cash Sweep Program.”
24          21.     The Wells Fargo Standard Bank Deposit Sweep sweeps customer cash to banks
25   that are affiliated with Wells Fargo. The Wells Fargo Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep sweeps
26   customers’ cash to banks that are both affiliated and unaffiliated with Wells Fargo. Regardless
27   of whether the banks are affiliated or unaffiliated with Wells Fargo, the interest rates paid to
28   Wells Fargo customers are determined by the rates charged at the Wells Fargo-affiliated banks.

                                                      4
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
               Case 3:24-cv-06696-DMR Document 1 Filed 09/24/24 Page 6 of 24



 1   Wells Fargo Advisors accomplishes this by directing and causing the unaffiliated banks

 2   participating in the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep program to credit interest on their deposits at

 3   the same rate as the affiliated banks. Under this regime, if unaffiliated banks are paying their

 4   non-Wells Fargo customers a higher interest rate than the affiliated banks, Wells Fargo Advisors

 5   will direct the unaffiliated banks to pay Wells Fargo customers the lower rate that is paid by

 6   Wells Fargo-affiliated banks.

 7          22.    More specifically, under the Wells Fargo Advisors Cash Sweep Program,

 8   uninvested cash balances in customers’ accounts are swept into interest-bearing deposit accounts

 9   (i.e., the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep or the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep) or, “if available,”

10   stable-value money market mutual funds (“Money Market Funds”). The Money Market Funds at

11   issue are registered with the SEC pursuant to the Investment Company Act of 1940.

12          23.    Wells Fargo has control and discretion over whether customers are deemed

13   “eligible” for each of the Cash Sweep Program options, and if money market funds are

14   “available,” and as a result, which Cash Sweep Program is selected for the customer. As

15   currently stated in Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep Disclosure Statement:

16                 When you open your account, or you select an ineligible Cash
                   Sweep Option, your Cash Sweep Option will be (and any cash
17                 balances will be transferred to) the primary Cash Sweep Option for
                   your account type. . . . If you decide to enroll in a new product or
18
                   service that doesn’t offer your current Cash Sweep Option, your
19                 new Cash Sweep Option will become the Expanded Bank Deposit
                   Sweep if you are eligible (if not, your Cash Sweep Option will be
20                 an available Money Market Fund selected by us) unless you select
                   a different available Cash Sweep Option.
21
            24.    Similarly, during most of the relevant period, Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep
22
     Disclosure Statement stated:
23
                   When you open your account, or you select an ineligible Cash
24
                   Sweep Vehicle, your Cash Sweep Vehicle will be (and any cash
25                 balances will be transferred to) the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep
                   if you are eligible (if not, your Cash Sweep Vehicle will be (and
26                 any cash balances will be transferred to) the Standard Bank
                   Deposit Sweep, or an available Money Market Fund selected by
27                 us).
28
            25.    Wells Fargo controls and has discretion over: (a) each customer’s “eligibility” for
                                                    5
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                Case 3:24-cv-06696-DMR Document 1 Filed 09/24/24 Page 7 of 24



 1   each sweep program vehicle and whether the customer’s cash is swept into the Expanded Bank

 2   Deposit Sweep, the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep, or Money Market Funds; (b) the

 3   characteristics and parameters of each of the available Sweep Cash Program options (Money

 4   Market Funds, the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep, and the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep); (c) if

 5   deposited into a Bank Deposit Sweep, the banks in which customers’ swept cash is deposited; (d)

 6   if invested in Money Market Fund holdings, the specific share class of the Money Market

 7   Fund(s) invested in; (e) the rates of interest paid on the Cash Sweep Program deposits (including

 8   because they are set by banks affiliated with Wells Fargo and in consultation with Wells Fargo

 9   Advisors); and (f) the speed at which uninvested cash is swept into sweep vehicles (with Wells

10   Fargo Advisors retaining any interest earned (generally at the Federal Funds rate) on cash

11   balances awaiting disbursement or prior to such balances being swept into a cash sweep vehicle).

12            26.     Due to Wells Fargo’s control and discretion over investors’ cash sweep holdings

13   and the returns on such holdings, Wells Fargo owes a fiduciary duty to all of its customers with

14   cash in sweep accounts, which includes a duty to act in their best interests, and to place such best

15   interests ahead of its own self-interest. Wells Fargo breached that fiduciary duty when it swept

16   client cash into Cash Sweep Program vehicles that paid customers unreasonably low interest

17   rates.

18            B.      The SEC Is Investigating Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep Practices

19            27.     Wells Fargo is currently under regulatory scrutiny for under-payment of interest
20   rates in cash sweep accounts and related misconduct. In the fall of 2023, Wells Fargo disclosed
21   that the SEC is investigating it over the cash sweep options provided to its advisory clients.
22            28.     On July 12, 2024, Wells Fargo disclosed on an earnings call that it was raising the
23   rates in its Cash Sweep Program held by advisory brokerage customers and stated that it
24   anticipates that the change will reduce its earnings by approximately $350 million annually.
25   Wells Fargo described this rate change as “better align[ing] rates with rates paid in money
26   market funds.”
27            29.     On August 1, 2024, Wells Fargo filed a quarterly report in which it disclosed
28   details about the “Advisory Account Cash Sweep Investigation.” Specifically, Wells Fargo

                                                       6
                                        CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
               Case 3:24-cv-06696-DMR Document 1 Filed 09/24/24 Page 8 of 24



 1   disclosed that the SEC “has undertaken an investigation regarding the cash sweep options that

 2   the Company provides to investment advisory clients at account opening,” and Wells Fargo “is

 3   in resolution discussions with the SEC, although there can be no assurance as to the outcome of

 4   these discussions.”

 5          C.      Wells Fargo Advisors’ Duties to Its Clients

 6          30.     Wells Fargo Advisors is a registered investment advisor bound by the fiduciary
 7   duties imposed on it by the Investment Advisors Act of 1940, including duties of care and
 8   loyalty. This includes a duty for Wells Fargo Advisors to act in the best interests of its clients,
 9   and to place the best interests of its customers ahead of its own self-interest. Similar duties are
10   imposed on Wells Fargo Advisors under principles of broker-dealer law.
11          31.     Wells Fargo Advisors has an investment advisor relationship with the members of
12   the Class. Wells Fargo Advisors has discretion over the amount of interest secured or paid to
13   Wells Fargo customers.
14          32.     In addition, Wells Fargo Advisors also acts as an agent for its customers. The
15   Wells Fargo Cash Sweep Disclosure Statement provides that “Wells Fargo Advisors will act as
16   your agent in establishing and maintaining the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs, including
17   making deposits to and withdrawals from the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs.” The disclosures
18   further state that a customer’s “first deposit into the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep or
19   Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep will constitute [the customer’s] appointment of Wells Fargo
20   Advisors as [the customer’s] agent in connection with the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep or
21   Expanded Bank Sweep.”
22          D.      Wells Fargo Is Contractually Obligated to Pay a Reasonable Rate of Interest
                    on Retirement Accounts
23
            33.     Pursuant to Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. Traditional IRA Custodial Agreement and
24
     Disclosures, Wells Fargo IRA customers and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. agree that “[a]ssets of the
25
     IRA may be invested in deposits of Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. (or an affiliate) that bear a
26
     reasonable rate of interest.”
27
            34.     Accordingly, Wells Fargo and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. have explicitly agreed to
28

                                                     7
                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                 Case 3:24-cv-06696-DMR Document 1 Filed 09/24/24 Page 9 of 24



 1   pay a “reasonable rate of interest” on the cash sweep accounts of their retirement account clients.

 2           35.     This contractual obligation is in conformity with Internal Revenue Code Section

 3   4975, the provisions of which apply to Wells Fargo’s IRA accounts. Specifically, Internal

 4   Revenue Code Section 4975 taxes “prohibited transactions,” including when an IRA plan

 5   sponsor engages in transactions with a “disqualified person who is a fiduciary whereby he deals

 6   with the income or assets of a plan in his own interest or for his own account.” 26 U.S.C. §

 7   4975(c).

 8           36.     A “disqualified person” includes those “providing services to the plan.”           26

 9   U.S.C. § 4975(e)(2)(B). This would include a bank that holds client assets and an advisory firm

10   that determines which bank will hold those assets, including Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. and Wells

11   Fargo Advisors.

12           37.     One safe harbor to the taxation of prohibited transactions is “the investment of all

13   or part of a plan’s assets in deposits which bear a reasonable interest rate in a bank or similar

14   financial institution.” 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(4). These provisions explicitly target situations

15   where a firm might attempt to benefit from holding its client funds by paying them unreasonably

16   low interest rates, and they are instead required to pay a “reasonable interest rate.” Accordingly,

17   under 26 U.S.C. § 4975, Defendants were required to pay a reasonable interest rate to retirement

18   account clients.

19           38.     In the context of accounts governed by 26 U.S.C. § 4975(c), the U.S. Department

20   of Labor defined a “reasonable rate” by considering fair market rates and similar benchmarks,

21   including “short-term rates available to other customers of the bank, those offered by other

22   banks, those available from money market funds, those applicable to short-term instruments such

23   as repurchase agreements, or by reference to a benchmark such as sovereign short term debt

24   (e.g., in the U.S., treasury bills).”

25           39.     The U.S. Treasury regulations include a similar requirement where Wells Fargo

26   “invests plan assets in deposits in itself or its affiliates.” 26 CFR § 54.5975-6(b)(3)(i). In those

27   circumstances, the parties’ agreement “must name” the bank and “state that [the bank] may make

28   investments in deposits which bear a reasonable rate of interest in itself (or in an affiliate).” Id.

                                             CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 1          40.      In sum, federal law requires that Wells Fargo pay its retirement account clients a

 2   “reasonable” interest rate.

 3          E.       Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep Contracts Include an Implied Covenant of Good
                     Faith and Fair Dealing
 4
            41.      Under New York law—which governs Wells Fargo customers’ agreements
 5
     regarding their cash sweep accounts—all contracts contain an implied covenant of good faith and
 6
     fair dealing, which encompasses any promises which a reasonable person in the position of the
 7
     promisee would be justified in understanding were included.
 8
            42.      This implied covenant includes a pledge that neither party shall do anything that
 9
     will have the effect of destroying or injuring the right of the other party to receive the fruits of
10
     the contract.
11
            43.      The current Wells Fargo Cash Sweep Disclosure Statement refers to Defendant
12
     Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC as “Wells Fargo Advisors”; it refers to banks affiliated with
13
     Wells Fargo as the “Affiliated Banks”; and it refers to banks unaffiliated with Wells Fargo as the
14
     “Unaffiliated Banks.”
15
            44.      The Wells Fargo Cash Sweep Disclosure Statement includes the following terms:
16
     “By making the Cash Sweep Program available, Wells Fargo Advisors assumes no obligation to
17
     seek or negotiate interest rates in excess of any reasonable rate of interest the Affiliated Banks
18
     are willing to credit.” While this language is phrased to disclaim responsibility to seek a rate “in
19
     excess of” a reasonable rate of interest, the term implicitly commits to pay at least a “reasonable
20
     rate” of interest on cash sweep accounts.
21
            45.      Wells Fargo’s Cash Sweep Disclosure Statement also includes the following term:
22
     “due to the contractual arrangements in place between the Unaffiliated Banks and the Clearing
23
     Agent, the rates paid out to clients will be substantially lower than the Federal Funds Effective
24
     Rate and will not increase as quickly as the Federal Funds Effective Rate.” This term indicates
25
     that there is a linkage between the interest rate paid on Wells Fargo cash sweep accounts and the
26
     Federal Funds Effective Rate and that, if the Federal Funds Effective Rate rises, so will the
27
     interest rate paid out to clients in cash sweep accounts.
28

 1          46.     Class members’ claim under the breach of the implied covenant of good faith and

 2   fair dealing is brought solely on behalf of individuals who do not have a contract expressly

 3   providing for Wells Fargo’s payment of a “reasonable rate” of interest on their sweep account

 4   balances (such as in an advisory or IRA agreement). Such claim is brought on behalf of non-

 5   advisory and non-IRA retail customers of Wells Fargo (the “Non-IRA Subclass”). Accordingly,

 6   the conduct and resulting injury alleged by the Non-IRA Subclass is not identical to, and such

 7   claim is not duplicative of, any asserted contractual claim on behalf of those Subclass members.

 8          F.      Wells Fargo Breached Its Fiduciary Duties, Contractual Obligations, and the
                    Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing, and Thereby Profited At
 9                  Its Clients’ Expense
10          47.     Wells Fargo breached and continues to breach its duties to secure reasonable
11   interest rates for its clients’ deposits, its contractual obligations, and the implied covenant of
12   good faith and fair dealing, because the interest it paid on its clients’ cash deposits was and is not
13   reasonable.

            49.     As set forth above, from as far back as 2014 through the present, for customers
 9
     with up to $999,999 in assets at Wells Fargo, Wells Fargo paid as little as .01% in interest, and
10
     only up to .15%, with that rate falling back to .02% starting in September 2024.
11
            50.     The U.S. Department of Labor has provided the following definition of a
12
     “reasonable” rate of interest:
13
                    A “reasonable” rate of interest means a rate of interest
14                  determinable by reference to short-term rates available to other
                    clients of the bank, those offered by other banks, those available
15                  from money market funds, those applicable to short-term
                    instruments such as repurchase agreements, or by reference to a
16                  benchmark such as sovereign short term debt (e.g., in the U.S.,
                    treasury bills), all in the jurisdiction where the rate is being
17                  evaluated.
18   68 Fed. Reg. 34646 (2003).
19          51.     The Internal Revenue Service similarly defines an “arm’s-length interest rate” as:
20                  a rate of interest which was charged, or would have been charged,
                    at the time the indebtedness arose, in independent transactions with
21                  or between unrelated parties under similar circumstances.
22   26 CFR § 1.482-2(a)(2).
23          52.     Under these terms, and any prudent understanding of what a “reasonable” rate of
24   interest is, Wells Fargo did not secure or pay a reasonable rate of interest to its customers,
25   including Plaintiff and Class members. This is supported by reference to other leading indicators
26   of interest rates being paid during this time period.
27                  1.      The Federal Funds Rate Benchmark
28          53.     The Federal Funds Rate benchmark demonstrates that the interest rate paid to

 1   Wells Fargo cash sweep accountholders was not reasonable. The federal funds market consists

 2   of domestic unsecured borrowings by depository institutions from other depository institutions

 3   and certain other entities, primarily government-sponsored enterprises. In other words, it is the

 4   market of unsecured borrowing transactions, principally between banks. The effective Federal

 5   Funds Rate is calculated as a volume-weighted median of such overnight federal funds

 6   transactions.

 8   rate of 5.33% as of August 28, 2024, for example. The chart below shows the stark and

 9   prolonged increase in the Federal Funds Rate over the past several years. By contrast, the

24                   2.     The Interest Rates on Sovereign Short-Term Debt Benchmark
25          55.      The yield on short-term U.S. Treasury Bills also demonstrates that the interest rate
